interventions.label: Cash transfers and income support increases
interventions.summary: Narrative review of high-income countries reports cash transfers reduce household food insecurity (for example a Canadian child benefit cut it by about 2.4 percentage points).

interventions.label: Food vouchers and grocery subsidies (SNAP-style)
interventions.summary: SNAP-type food entitlements are associated with reduced food insecurity, though rates among recipients stay high; no Australian voucher evaluation found.

interventions.label: Food banks and food pantries
interventions.summary: Review finds limited evidence of impact; users often remain severely food insecure and stigma limits use (Foodbank 2025: 45% cite shame).

interventions.label: Community meals and community kitchens
interventions.summary: Studies are mostly small and descriptive, reporting cooking skills and social benefits; gains are fragile and participation low.

interventions.label: School meal and breakfast programs
interventions.summary: The review excluded free meal provision; it cites a single study where a school breakfast programme improved household food security. No Victorian evaluation or sourced cost found.

interventions.label: Community food co-ops and social grocers
interventions.summary: Box Divvy members reported about 23% lower food insecurity after joining (self-reported, no clear control group); Melbourne Community Grocer produce was about 40% cheaper in a small case study.

caveats: Definitions differ: Foodbank Hunger Report (33% of households, 2025, Ipsos online survey) and ABS 2023 (13.2% of households, 10-item USDA module) and VPHS (8% of Victorian adults ran out of food, 2022) measure different things and must not be plotted as one series.
No 2019-to-latest trend series was obtained from an opened primary source; Foodbank 2025 report page gives only 2023-2025 comparisons.
Victorian statewide figure for Hunger Report 2025 not found in an opened source; Victorian figures seen only in search snippets or secondary news (not recorded as indicators).
Melbourne Institute Poverty Lines (March/June quarter 2026) pages were unavailable to us; poverty lines used are ACOSS/UNSW 2022-23 values from a media release reprint.
ABS HES figures are from the 2015-16 release only (newer HES results not located); healthy food basket data is Victorian 2012-2014 only; no current Melbourne basket cost found.
SEIFA values are ABS SA2 areas (2021), not suburbs; SA2 boundaries differ from suburb boundaries and several suburbs split into multiple SA2s. Lower score means more disadvantage.

Student weekly living cost estimates for Melbourne come only from provider/marketing pages seen in search snippets and were not opened; recorded as not found. Universities Australia survey itself was not opened.
Intervention evidence rests on one narrative review (2018) plus small Australian studies; no sourced cost-per-person figures found; community fridges: no evaluation found.
Source guidance on setting a food budget as a share of income was not found; do not present any rule-of-thumb as sourced.
